body: Ghana is mostly flat with red soil, with some regions featuring hills and mountains. Tropical vegetation and palms are common especially in the south.
Ghana is a patriotic country where many objects are painted in the national flag’s colours: red, yellow, green, sometimes including the black star.
Road lines in Ghana are always white, but many paved roads might not have any road lines at all.
Ghana typically uses wooden poles with 3 insulators mounted on a metallic crossbar.
Most unpaved roads in a dry savannah landscape are found north of Wa, including the Yendi-Nkwanta road and Salaga-Tamale road with distinct soil.
The road connecting Sawla with the N10 features crisp new road lines running east-west through lush savannah, with solid or dashed middle lines.
The Salaga-Tamale road to Kpalbusi is a dirt road with moody overcast coverage and very dark purple-brown soil.
The road between Nkwanta and Domanko is unpaved, with a powerline running close east or northeast, through lush savannah characteristic of central Ghana.
On a section of the N2 east of Lake Volta, there is a ridgeline to the southeast near the road, which runs southwest-northeast under overcast grey skies.
The coastal area east of Accra on the N1 highway is distinctively flat and wide open with less vegetation and sometimes a dry appearance.
The N1 road section near Elubo has very new dark asphalt with crisp middle lines and no outer lines, surrounded by dense vegetation with occasional palm trees.
The Keta Lagoon in southeast Ghana is visible along the nearby road, with sandy soil and a coastal atmosphere.
Nature reserves and sanctuaries in Ghana feature a unique white Google car with side mirrors visible and the characteristic ‘Ghana tape’.
The Ankasa Game Reserve uses a unique Google car with a visible front, street view vinyl roof, and ‘Ghana tape’ marked on it.
The Boabeng Fiema Monkey Sanctuary Google car lacks the ‘Ghana tape’ and roof rack but has a visible black right side mirror. The red soil and vegetation remain good regional clues.
All regular road coverage in Ghana was made with a unique Google car featuring a roof rack with a piece of black tape and a red rectangle on the hood, aiding in regional identification.
Ghana uses white licence plates on normal vehicles and yellow plates for commercial vehicles, which can be long or short. Plate colours help distinguish vehicle types.
Taxis in Ghana typically have multicoloured body panels with fenders and quarter panels always coloured orange-yellow.
